summary.text: Writing $m=(p-1)/2$ and $C=m!$, Wilson’s theorem gives $C^2=(-1)^{m+1}$; for $p\equiv3\pmod4$, the columns can be indexed by signed nonzero quadratic residues so that a character-product parity argument selects an odd principal minor of a skew-symmetric Paley-type matrix, forcing the determinant to vanish (with the accompanying symmetric matrix invertible by a Vandermonde factorization). For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, Euler’s criterion reduces the matrix modulo $p$ to $((x_i-y_j)^m)$, whose binomial expansion factors into a Vandermonde matrix and a nonsingular coefficient matrix, the latter using $C^2=-1$ to show $\prod_j y_j\ne1$; hence the original integer determinant is nonzero.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p=p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, where \(n\ge 2\), and put
\[
 m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=m!.
\]
Since \(n\ge2\), we have \(p\ge3\), so \(p\) is odd and \(p=2m+1\). Let \(\chi\) denote the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_p\), extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). Because \(p\) is prime, this is the Legendre symbol, and hence also the Jacobi symbol appearing in the definition of the sequence. Thus the matrix defining \(a(n)\) is
\[
 M=\bigl(\chi(i^2-Cj)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}.
\]
(The entries are integers in \(\{-1,0,1\}\).) We prove that
\[
 \det M=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]

We first collect several facts that will be used in the two congruence classes.

### 1. The half-factorial congruence

Wilson's theorem gives
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p.
\]
Split the factors \(1,2,\dots,2m\) into the lower half \(1,\dots,m\) and the upper half \(m+1,\dots,2m\). Modulo \(p=2m+1\), the upper-half factors are
\[
 m+1,m+2,\dots,2m\equiv -m,-(m-1),\dots,-1.
\]
Their product is therefore \((-1)^m m!\). Consequently
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv m!\,(-1)^m m!=(-1)^m C^2\pmod p.
\]
Comparing this with Wilson's theorem yields
\[
 C^2=(-1)^{m+1}\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{1}
\]
In particular,
\[
 \begin{cases}
 C^2=1,&p\equiv3\pmod4\quad(m\text{ odd}),\\
 C^2=-1,&p\equiv1\pmod4\quad(m\text{ even}).
 \end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
In either case \(C\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\).

We will also use that the nonzero squares in \(\mathbb F_p\) are precisely
\[
 Q=\{1^2,2^2,\dots,m^2\}. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, these \(m\) elements are distinct: if \(i^2=j^2\) with \(1\le i,j\le m\), then \(i\equiv j\) or \(i\equiv-j\pmod p\). The first gives \(i=j\), while the second is impossible because \(0<i+j\le2m<p\). Every nonzero square has two square roots \(u\) and \(-u\), exactly one of whose standard representatives lies between \(1\) and \(m\), proving (3). Equivalently, \(|Q|=m\).

### 2. A Paley-matrix lemma for \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

For this section suppose \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is odd and \(\chi(-1)=-1\). Index matrices by the set \(Q\) of nonzero squares, and define
\[
 A_{x,y}=\chi(x-y),\qquad B_{x,y}=\chi(x+y)\qquad(x,y\in Q).
\]
We need four properties of these matrices.

First, \(A\) is skew-symmetric. In fact,
\[
 A_{y,x}=\chi(y-x)=\chi(-(x-y))=\chi(-1)\chi(x-y)=-A_{x,y}.
\]
Second, \(B\) is symmetric, since addition is commutative.

Third, \(A\) and \(B\) commute. For fixed \(x,y\in Q\),
\[
 (AB)_{x,y}=\sum_{r\in Q}\chi(x-r)\chi(r+y)
 =\sum_{r\in Q}\chi((x-r)(r+y)).
\]
The map
\[
 r\longmapsto \frac{xy}{r}
\]
is a permutation of \(Q\), because \(x,y,r\) are all nonzero squares. Under this substitution, the product in the character becomes
\[
 \left(x-\frac{xy}{r}\right)\left(\frac{xy}{r}+y\right)
 =\frac{xy}{r^2}(x+r)(r-y).

a
\]
Here \(xy/r^2\) is a nonzero square, so its quadratic character is \(1\). Thus the corresponding summand is
\[
 \chi(x+r)\chi(r-y).
\]
Summing over \(r\in Q\) gives \((BA)_{x,y}\). Hence
\[
 AB=BA. \tag{4}
\]

Fourth, \(B\) is nonsingular over \(\mathbb Q\). We prove this by reducing its integral entries modulo \(p\). Enumerate \(Q\) as distinct elements \(r_0,\dots,r_{m-1}\). Euler's criterion says that in \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \chi(t)\equiv t^m
\]
for every \(t\in\mathbb F_p\), including \(t=0\). Hence the reduction of \(B\) modulo \(p\) is the matrix
\[
 H_{ij}=(r_i+r_j)^m.
\]
Every \(r_i\in Q\) satisfies \(r_i^m=1\). Expanding by the binomial theorem and combining the terms of degrees \(0\) and \(m\), we obtain a factorization
\[
 H=VD,
\]
where
\[
 V_{ik}=r_i^k\qquad(0\le k<m)
\]
is a Vandermonde matrix, and, after a permutation of its rows, \(D\) is the product of the transpose of a Vandermonde matrix in the \(r_j\)'s and the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries
\[
 2,\binom m1,\binom m2,\dots,\binom m{m-1}.
\]
More explicitly, the binomial expansion is
\[
 (r_i+r_j)^m
 =2+\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\binom mk r_i^k r_j^{m-k},

a
\]
so the exponents of \(r_j\) are \(0,m-1,m-2,\dots,1\), merely a permutation of \(0,1,\dots,m-1\).

The determinant of \(V\) is
\[
 \prod_{i<j}(r_j-r_i)\ne0
\]
because the \(r_i\)'s are distinct. The same is true of the row-permuted transposed Vandermonde matrix. Also none of the displayed diagonal entries vanishes modulo \(p\). Certainly \(2\ne0\), and for \(1\le k<m<p\), \(p\nmid\binom mk\): otherwise, from
\[
 \binom mk k!(m-k)!=m!
\]
we would obtain \(p\mid m!\), impossible because every factor of \(m!\) is less than \(p\). Therefore \(\det H\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). It follows that the original integral determinant \(\det B\) is nonzero, and hence \(B\) is invertible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Define
\[
 K=B^{-1}A.
\]
Using symmetry of \(B\), skew-symmetry of \(A\), and (4), we find
\[
 K^T=A^T(B^{-1})^T=(-A)B^{-1}=-B^{-1}A=-K. \tag{5}
\]
Thus \(K\) is skew-symmetric.

We now derive the column-selection consequence that will force the desired determinant to vanish. Suppose a function \(c:Q\to\mathbb F_p\) satisfies
\[
 c(q)=q\quad\text{or}\quad c(q)=-q
\]
for every \(q\in Q\), and put
\[
 S=\{q\in Q:c(q)=q\}.
\]
Consider the matrix
\[
 N_{x,q}=\chi(x-c(q)).
\]
If \(q\in S\), its \(q\)-th column is the \(q\)-th column of \(A\). If \(q\notin S\), then \(c(q)=-q\), and its \(q\)-th column is the \(q\)-th column of \(B\). Let \(E\) be the matrix whose \(q\)-th column is the \(q\)-th column of \(K\) for \(q\in S\), and the \(q\)-th standard basis vector for \(q\notin S\). Since \(BK=A\), we have
\[
 N=BE. \tag{6}
\]
After simultaneously ordering the indices so that those in \(S\) come first, \(E\) has block form
\[
 E=\begin{pmatrix}K_{S,S}&0\\ *&I\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \det E=\det K_{S,S}. \tag{7}
\]
The principal submatrix \(K_{S,S}\) is skew-symmetric by (5). If \(|S|\) is odd, then
\[
 \det K_{S,S}=\det(K_{S,S}^T)=\det(-K_{S,S})=(-1)^{|S|}\det K_{S,S}=-\det K_{S,S}.
\]
Over \(\mathbb Q\), this implies \(\det K_{S,S}=0\). Equations (6) and (7) then give
\[
 \det N=0. \tag{8}
\]
We will apply this with a specially constructed \(c\) for which \(|S|\) is odd.

### 3. Vanishing when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

Assume now that \(p=4k+3\), so \(m=2k+1\). By (2), \(C^2=1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). For \(1\le j\le m\), set
\[
 z_j=Cj\in\mathbb F_p.
\]
These elements are nonzero. Because \(\chi(-1)=-1\), exactly one of \(z_j\) and \(-z_j\) is a square: multiplication by \(-1\) reverses quadratic character. Let \(q_j\in Q\) be that square. Thus
\[
 q_j=z_j\quad\text{or}\quad q_j=-z_j. \tag{9}
\]
The \(q_j\)'s are distinct. Indeed, if \(q_i=q_j\), then (9) gives \(z_i=z_j\) or \(z_i=-z_j\). Since \(C\ne0\), the first yields \(i\equiv j\pmod p\), hence \(i=j\) because \(1\le i,j<p\). The second yields \(i+j\equiv0\pmod p\), which is impossible because \(0<i+j\le2m=p-1\). Since both the set of indices and \(Q\) have \(m\) elements, \(j\mapsto q_j\) is a bijection.

Use this bijection to define \(c:Q\to\mathbb F_p\) by
\[
 c(q_j)=z_j.
\]
Then, by (9), \(c(q)=q\) or \(-q\) for every \(q\). Let
\[
 S=\{q:c(q)=q\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(S\) consists of those \(q_j\) for which \(z_j\) is a square. We show that \(|S|\) is odd.

First calculate the product of all the \(c(q)\)'s:
\[
 \prod_{q\in Q}c(q)=\prod_{j=1}^m Cj=C^m m!=C^{m+1}.
\]
Since \(m+1=2(k+1)\) and \(C^2=1\), this product is \(1\). Applying the multiplicative character gives
\[
 \prod_{q\in Q}\chi(c(q))=1. \tag{10}
\]
Each factor is \(1\) or \(-1\). Since \(-1\ne1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), (10) says that the number of factors equal to \(-1\) is even. Those factors correspond exactly to nonsquare values \(c(q)\), namely to the complement \(Q\setminus S\). Hence \(|Q\setminus S|\) is even. But \(|Q|=m\) is odd, so \(|S|\) is odd.

The Paley column-selection result (8) therefore applies and gives
\[
 \det\bigl(\chi(x-c(q))\bigr)_{x,q\in Q}=0. \tag{11}
\]
Reindex the rows by \(x=i^2\), \(1\le i\le m\), using (3), and the columns by \(q=q_j\). Because \(c(q_j)=Cj\), the reindexed entries in (11) are exactly
\[
 \chi(i^2-Cj).
\]
Reindexing rows and columns can change a determinant only by multiplication by signs, and therefore preserves its being zero. Thus
\[
 \det M=0
\]
whenever \(p\equiv3\pmod4\).

### 4. A general determinant factorization

To prove nonvanishing in the other congruence class, we establish a determinant lemma. Let \(F\) be a field, let \(m>0\), and let
\[
 x_0,\dots,x_{m-1},\qquad y_0,\dots,y_{m-1}\in F
\]
satisfy:

1. the \(x_i\)'s are distinct;
2. the \(y_j\)'s are distinct;
3. \(x_i^m=1\) for every \(i\);
4. \(\binom mk\ne0\) in \(F\) for \(1\le k<m\);
5. \(\prod_j y_j\ne1\).

Then
\[
 \det\bigl((x_i-y_j)^m\bigr)\ne0. \tag{12}
\]

To prove this, expand
\[
 (x_i-y_j)^m=(x_i+(-y_j))^m.
\]
The term with exponent \(m\) in \(x_i\) equals \(x_i^m=1\), so it can be combined with the term having exponent \(0\). This gives the factorization
\[
 \bigl((x_i-y_j)^m\bigr)=V_xD,
\]
where \((V_x)_{ik}=x_i^k\) for \(0\le k<m\), and
\[
 D_{k,j}=
 \begin{cases}
 1+(-y_j)^m,&k=0,\\
 \binom mk(-y_j)^{m-k},&1\le k<m.
 \end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
The Vandermonde determinant of \(V_x\) is nonzero by distinctness of the \(x_i\)'s. It remains to prove \(\det D\ne0\).

Put \(z_j=-y_j\), and let \(P\) be the matrix whose rows, in order, have exponents
\[
 0,m-1,m-2,\dots,1;

a
\]
that is,
\[
 P_{0j}=1,\qquad P_{kj}=z_j^{m-k}\quad(1\le k<m).
\]
This is a row permutation of a Vandermonde matrix in the distinct \(z_j\)'s, so \(\det P\ne0\). Let \(P'\) be obtained from \(P\) by replacing its first row by \((z_j^m)_j\). By linearity of the determinant in the first row, the matrix obtained by replacing the first row of \(P\) by \((1+z_j^m)_j\) has determinant
\[
 \det P+\det P'. \tag{14}
\]
Factor \(z_j\) from column \(j\) of \(P'\). What remains has row exponents
\[
 m-1,m-2,\dots,0,
\]
which is obtained from the row order \(0,m-1,m-2,\dots,1\) of \(P\) by moving the first row to the end. This row cycle has sign \((-1)^{m-1}\). Therefore
\[
 \det P'=(-1)^{m-1}\det P\prod_jz_j.
\]
Since \(z_j=-y_j\),
\[
 \prod_jz_j=(-1)^m\prod_jy_j,
\]
and hence
\[
 \det P'=-\det P\prod_jy_j.
\]
Thus (14) equals
\[
 \det P\left(1-\prod_jy_j\right), \tag{15}
\]
which is nonzero by assumptions 2 and 5. Finally, the matrix \(D\) in (13) is obtained from this row-modified \(P\) by multiplying row \(k\) by \(\binom mk\) for \(k>0\) (and row \(0\) by \(1\)). All these multipliers are nonzero by assumption 4. Therefore \(\det D\ne0\), proving (12).

### 5. Nonvanishing when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)

Assume \(p=4k+1\), so \(m=2k\). By (2),
\[
 C^2=-1\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{16}
\]
Define, for \(1\le i,j\le m\),
\[
 x_i=i^2,\qquad y_j=Cj
\]
as elements of \(\mathbb F_p\). The \(x_i\)'s are distinct by (3), and the \(y_j\)'s are distinct because \(C\ne0\) and the integers \(1,\dots,m\) are distinct modulo \(p\). Moreover each \(x_i\) is a nonzero square, so Euler's criterion gives
\[
 x_i^m=1. \tag{17}
\]
As above, \(\binom mr\ne0\pmod p\) for \(1\le r<m\), because \(m<p\).

It remains to check the product condition in the determinant lemma. We have
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^m y_j=C^m m!=C^{m+1}. \tag{18}
\]
This is not \(1\). Indeed, if \(C^{m+1}=1\), then, since \(m=2k\),
\[
 C^{m+1}=(C^2)^kC=(-1)^kC=1.
\]
Squaring would give \(C^2=1\), contradicting (16), because \(p>2\) and hence \(-1\ne1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\).

All hypotheses of the determinant lemma now hold, and therefore
\[
 \det\bigl((x_i-y_j)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}\ne0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{19}
\]
By Euler's criterion, for every \(t\in\mathbb F_p\), the integer \(\chi(t)\), reduced modulo \(p\), equals \(t^m\). Thus the reduction modulo \(p\) of the original integer matrix \(M\) is exactly
\[
 \bigl((i^2-Cj)^m\bigr)=\bigl((x_i-y_j)^m\bigr).
\]
If \(\det M\) were zero as an integer, its reduction modulo \(p\) would be zero, contradicting (19). Hence
\[
 \det M\ne0
\]
when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\).

### 6. Conclusion

Every odd prime is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\pmod4\). For \(n\ge2\), the prime \(p_n\) is odd. Section 3 proves that the determinant defining \(a(n)\) vanishes when \(p_n\equiv3\pmod4\), while Section 5 proves that it does not vanish when \(p_n\equiv1\pmod4\). Therefore, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
 \boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }.
\]
